role: Independent web developer; no library implementation edits
goal: Build a static immutable-expense dashboard with a custom AssemblyScript category count/total view; prove browser/Python parity using the identical Wasm artifact.
initial_assumptions: BrowserDatabase is an asynchronous in-memory database in a dedicated worker; export is needed before reload.
A custom module needs direct asc compilation plus a descriptor/digest manifest, not npm run build discovery.
The SDK can be imported from a custom source nested under views/; compiler module resolution may require that location.
rows() provides key/state/result records; browser exported resolved records need Document conversion for Python ingestion.
SDK example sources are authoring references; host/library implementation will be read only after a documented workflow blocks, with assumptions recorded first.

chronology.outcome: README gives explicit custom compiler link and static browser asset-copy path. No ancestor AGENTS.md found.

chronology.action: Read docs/portable.html authoring/browser/export sections; docs/api.html; views/assembly/examples/metrics.ts for structured count state.
chronology.outcome: Enough public guidance to implement a count/total reducer without reading browser or native source.

source_fallbacks.initial_assumption: The replay boolean might be matches; guide only says replay reports equivalence and prints the whole object.
source_fallbacks.result: Search included docs/static/playground.js:117, a public example that checks result.equivalent. A separate live BrowserDatabase call confirmed the complete return object.

failures.classification: Developer harness assumption; no claimed library defect
failures.assumption: Expected db.replay() equivalence boolean under matches; docs say reports equivalence but show whole result without schema.
failures.next_step: Inspect actual public replay response with a small browser snippet; no source fallback required.

failures.classification: Developer harness assumption contradicted by documented sequence semantics, not a product defect
failures.workaround: Compare retained identity/payload/source-position fields plus computation key/state/result; preserve original batch boundaries only if exact engine sequence equality is required.

findings.title: Browser return shapes need a compact reference
findings.observation: The guide gives executable browser integration and prose method summaries, but no replay return schema. My first assertion guessed matches; the real field is equivalent. The actual call succeeds.
findings.workaround: Inspect the returned object in Chromium, then use result.equivalent.
findings.proposal: Document replay() → {equivalent,documents,groups,module_sha256}; add concise signatures/result shapes for add, addMany, ingest, export, and stats, or provide TypeScript declarations.
findings.impact: One inspection/rerun; did not require reading host code or changing library behavior.

findings.title: Browser conflict type is embedded in a generic Error message
findings.observation: A conflicting resolved record rejects atomically, with a useful message. The JS error has name Error, so differentiating conflict from validation requires parsing a message prefix.

evidence.name: Error
evidence.message: DocumentConflict: document identity already has different contents or position

findings.workaround: Display the message for this small dashboard; do not branch on error class.
findings.proposal: Expose a stable error.code such as DocumentConflict and document the browser error contract; preserve the current descriptive message.
findings.impact: Relevant when an app offers retry/conflict recovery; no blocker for this dashboard.

findings.title: Custom modules require manual build and manifest scaffolding
findings.observation: The direct compiler command worked first try, but the app needed a long SDK-specific asc command plus a separate manifest program. npm run build intentionally covers only bundled modules, as README clearly explains.
findings.workaround: Adapt the documented command, relative SDK import, and manifest script into study-local files.
findings.proposal: Offer a documented script accepting custom source and output paths that applies pinned flags and writes the matching descriptor/digest manifest; keep current direct command as the transparent fallback.
findings.impact: Setup effort and copy/paste surface, not a compiler failure.

findings.title: Preserved records retain identity while local sequence numbers can change
findings.observation: I initially compared complete browser exports before and after restore; that failed because sequence is batch-local engine progress. Re-reading the nearby replay section clarified comparing key/state/result and retained identity fields.
findings.workaround: Compare id,payload,position,source for retained records, and key,state,result for computation. Do not compare sequence or cursor across workers/databases.
findings.proposal: Repeat a one-line note immediately beside browser ingest/export: exported sequence is informational and regenerated on import. Existing full explanation is accurate.
findings.impact: One harness correction; explicitly not a data-loss or parity defect.

outcome: Authored and compiled a category count/total view; built and exercised a local static dashboard in real Chromium; exact key/state/result parity with the native Python engine using identical Wasm bytes.
constraints_observed: No library, documentation, test, bundled artifact, or package file edits.
App, fixtures, compiled Wasm/manifest, copied browser runtime, evidence and verification scripts only under .build/ux-study/browser/.
Custom AssemblyScript compiler input only under views/.build/ux-study-browser/.
Only this study report under reports/ux-study/browser.json; no other study reports read or agents contacted.
No dependency installs, external publishing, or external service calls; browser requests served locally.

application.mapper: String category plus finite numeric amount emits category → amount; malformed shapes emit nothing. UI validates records before append/import.
application.reducer: Explicit {count,total} state; sequential addition; rejects invalid state/contributions and nonfinite overflow; merge disabled.
application.app_import_bound: One addMany/ingest batch, at most 1024 records; no automatic chunking in this study app.

browser_checks: restore preserves results, identities, payloads, and source positions
native_checks: identical Wasm SHA-256 in Chromium and Python View
native ingestion of downloaded resolved browser records
checkpoint and rebuild preserve computation and log bytes
plain-payload map/reduce parity across different batch boundaries
validation.sequence_interpretation: Sequences differ after restoring original 1/1/4/1 batches as one batch. IDs, payloads, source positions, key/state/result outputs match. This is explicitly documented behavior, not a defect.

intuitive_successes: README has a direct path to custom authoring, explains named build scope, and distinguishes browser memory from the Rust durable log.
The complete custom module example, public SDK helpers and structured metrics example were enough to author a new view without reading implementation internals.
Documented asc flags worked on the first compilation; descriptor extraction and digest manifest loaded in the worker on the first browser launch.
Asset copying via portable_assets().iterdir()/read_bytes() worked without path guessing or bundler setup.
Custom BrowserDatabase.connect({name,base}) worked on a plain Python static HTTP server.
rows, snapshot changes, replay, export, restored ingest and idempotent restore behaved as documented.
Conflict and oversized batch failures preserved existing state; the size-limit message states the actual 1024 bound.
Browser-to-Python Document conversion snippet worked for the custom view, not just the bundled example.
The exact custom bytes produced matching category counts, totals, state and key order in Chromium and Rust-native Python, including Unicode, zero and a negative credit.
limitations_of_study: Seven valid expense records and four groups; no throughput, sustained memory, crash recovery, arbitrary view correctness, or production readiness claim.
Amounts chosen for exact binary representability; this is a reproducibility check, not a decimal-currency arithmetic guarantee.
No network/offline persistence, IndexedDB, or multi-tab coordination tested; documented browser lifetime is in-memory.
Only real local Chromium used; no Safari or Firefox compatibility claim.
